extracted.intended_audience: general readers and theatre students/practitioners interested in Molière and stage comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and historical/contextual information relevant to staging, translating, adapting, or analysing Molière's Tartuffe — a 1664 comedic play often treated as a farce and satirical critique of hypocrisy. Useful for directors, translators, adaptors, students, and critics considering performance choices, censorship history, and comic technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification — comedy/farce
rubrics_metrics.description: Tartuffe is described as a theatrical comedy (more specifically, a farce) by Molière; characters such as Tartuffe, Elmire, and Orgon are considered among the greatest classical theatre roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations and productions should treat the piece as satirical comedy with farcical elements; staging, performance style, and direction should foreground comic timing, exaggerated situations, and character types appropriate to comedy/farce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal verse: alexandrines and rhyming couplets
rubrics_metrics.description: The play is written entirely in twelve-syllable lines (alexandrines) of rhyming couplets — 1,962 lines total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators and directors must decide whether to preserve the alexandrine/rhyming structure (affecting rhythm and comic timing) or to render the play into prose/free verse; preserving verse influences diction, pacing, and performative delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character construction — clear types embodying hypocrisy and gullibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Key characters (Tartuffe, Elmire, Orgon, Dorine, Damis, Mariane, Cléante) function as exemplars: Tartuffe as hypocritical devotee, Orgon as the bewitched gullible host, Dorine as wily maid/rasonneur, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting and performance should emphasize the archetypal qualities (hypocrisy, gullibility, reason, comic servant) so that social satire and interpersonal conflicts read clearly to audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic mechanism — incongruity and ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: A contemporary defence of the play argues that 'incongruity is the heart of the comic' and that outward show differing from reality (lying, disguise, dissimulation) is essentially comic; ridicule of vice discourages imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Productions should make the incongruity between appearance and reality evident and frame Tartuffe's actions as objects of ridicule so the audience perceives moral critique rather than endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot device: deus ex machina (royal intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The play ends with an unexpected benevolent intervention by the King (officer arrests Tartuffe instead of Orgon), a notable example of the classical deus ex machina plot device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adaptors/directors should decide how to handle or justify the twist ending in modern stagings (retain, update, or alter) because it reshapes the play's resolution and its political/theatrical implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic techniques for exposing hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: The play uses staging/eavesdropping (Orgon hiding under a table to listen), staged seduction by Elmire to reveal Tartuffe, and examples of reverse psychology by Tartuffe to manipulate other characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directorial and blocking choices should foreground these dramatic devices (concealment, staged encounters, overheard conversations) to clearly reveal character motives and to create comic irony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and sensitivity when satirising religion/power
rubrics_metrics.description: Tartuffe provoked immediate controversy and suppression (archbishop edict, temporary ban); Molière revised the play to appear more secular and less critical of religion to appease authorities; private performances occurred while public ones were banned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting or staging material that satirises religious or political institutions, practitioners should be aware of historical and contemporary sensitivities and may choose strategies (reframing, secularising, contextualising) to manage offence or censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation flexibility — relocating setting and updating social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern adaptations relocate the story (e.g., to African-American affluent Durham, Pakistani-Muslim Sparkhill, a feminist consultancy firm, 1950s Texas) and reimagine characters/professions (business guru, politician, consultancy co-CEOs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The play can be successfully adapted across cultures and eras; adaptors should map the story's central dynamics (hypocrisy, gullibility, power relations) onto contemporary equivalents while retaining comedic and thematic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific production considerations (stage, film, TV, radio, opera, audio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tartuffe has been produced in many media — stage productions (Comédie-Française, RSC), Broadway, film (1926, 1984), television adaptations, radio broadcasts, opera settings, and audio recordings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each medium demands different translation/adaptation choices (visual mise-en-scène for film, vocal nuance for radio, musical setting for opera) and will affect pacing, emphasis, and how comic elements are realized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation choices — fidelity to original verse vs modernization
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous translations exist (Richard Wilbur, Ranjit Bolt, Roger McGough, Ranjit Bolt's rhyming translations, etc.), some preserving rhyming couplets and verse forms, others modernizing language and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators must weigh fidelity to Molière's verse and period diction against intelligibility and contemporary comic effect; decisions will influence rhythm, comedic timing, and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signalling satire so audience discerns critique not endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenders of the play argued that Tartuffe's actions are worthy of ridicule and thus cannot be mistaken for endorsement; the comic must denote the absence of the rational so audiences see what to avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction, performance tone, and dramaturgy should make the satirical stance explicit—through staging, reaction of other characters, and comic framing—so viewers clearly perceive the play's moral critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production history and casting as indicators of interpretive lineage
rubrics_metrics.description: The play's long production history (Comédie-Française repertoire, notable productions and performers across centuries) shows a range of interpretive choices and the importance of star casting and company repertory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers and directors can consult past prominent productions for interpretive models; casting prominent actors in key roles and aligning with a company's repertory tradition can shape audience expectations and reception.
